scopes.issue: The phrase “may be exercised” was alleged to make the prescribed written-notice method merely “optional” or a “preferred choice,” but the court held that “may” referred to GSA’s discretion to exercise the option and did not make notice optional.
scopes.why: The clause’s grammar itself shows that “may” modifies the Optionee’s choice to exercise, while exercise must occur “by serving written notice” in the prescribed manner.

scopes.issue: The prescribed notice methods—certified or registered mail, personal delivery, or recognized private overnight courier—were disputed as to whether GSA’s email could qualify as the written notice required to exercise the option, and the court held that it could not.
scopes.needs: May 10,2007 email from Ms. Hoffman (Exhibit L)
scopes.why: Without the actual case-specific email, a reader cannot assess whether GSA’s purported exercise complied with the prescribed notice methods.

scopes.issue: The phrase “applies only to buildings to which the Replacement Cost Optional Coverage applies” was disputed over whether ordinance-compliance costs remained separate Additional Coverage or became part of replacement cost after the replacement-cost exclusion was excised.
scopes.why: The dispute requires the policy’s separate Additional Coverage, Replacement Cost, ordinance-cost exclusion, and coinsurance provisions to determine whether the costs remain separate from replacement cost.

scopes.issue: The grant for “increased costs incurred to comply with enforcement of an ordinance or law” was disputed over whether those costs were exclusively Additional Coverage or also fell within replacement cost after the exclusion was excised.
scopes.why: The grant alone does not establish exclusivity, which emerges only by comparing it with the policy’s Replacement Cost and ordinance-cost provisions.

scopes.issue: The phrase “value of Covered Property” was disputed over whether the replacement-cost value used to determine underinsurance included increased costs of complying with modern laws and ordinances.
scopes.why: Determining what constitutes the “value of Covered Property” requires the policy’s Covered Property definition, Replacement Cost provisions, and separate ordinance-cost Additional Coverage.

scopes.issue: The phrase “total amount of loss” was disputed over whether the loss to which the coinsurance percentage applies includes ordinance-compliance costs provided as Additional Coverage.
scopes.why: Whether “total amount of loss” includes ordinance-compliance costs requires reading the coinsurance calculation together with the policy provisions granting those costs as Additional Coverage.

scopes.issue: The term “Replacement Cost” was disputed after G.3.f was excised—State Auto read it to include law-and-ordinance costs in both the complex valuation and Building 1 loss, while Boardwalk read those costs as separate Additional Coverage.
scopes.why: The disputed scope of Replacement Cost after excision of G.3.f can be seen only by comparing Section G with the policy’s ordinance-cost Additional Coverage and coinsurance terms.

scopes.issue: The phrase “actual loss of Business Income” was disputed over whether Boardwalk could retain investment income earned from State Auto’s advance payment without an offset or whether that income had to be deducted from its business-income loss.
scopes.needs: Evidence of State Auto’s advance payment and Boardwalk’s resulting investment income
scopes.why: The clause does not reveal that Boardwalk invested an insurer advance and earned income whose treatment as an offset generated the dispute.

scopes.issue: The phrase “operating expenses ... necessary to resume ‘operations’” was disputed over whether saved depreciation was a noncontinuing expense deductible from rental-value benefits or merely a non-cash accounting figure that should not be deducted.
scopes.why: The treatment of depreciation turns on the policy’s selected rental-value coverage and its definitions, not merely the quoted general loss-determination provision.

scopes.issue: The endpoint “when the property ... should be repaired, rebuilt or replaced with reasonable speed and similar quality” was disputed over whether it meant the actual reconstruction date or a theoretical reconstruction period and whether insurer-caused litigation delay extended that period.
scopes.needs: Missouri-litigation records,non-waiver agreement,and reconstruction-delay evidence
scopes.why: The clause presents the endpoint standard, but the issue whether insurer-caused litigation delayed reconstruction requires the transaction-specific litigation and rebuilding record.

scopes.issue: The statement that Angie’s List “simply acts as a passive conduit,” construed with the Agreement’s firsthand-review and no-endorsement provisions, was disputed as collectively requiring a provider-rating system unshaped by paid ranking changes or suppression of negative reviews.
scopes.why: The firsthand-review and no-endorsement provisions elsewhere in the Membership Agreement are needed to derive the collective requirement that the rating system remain unshaped by paid ranking changes or suppressed reviews.

scopes.issue: The statement that Angie’s List “does not endorse” service providers, construed with the Agreement’s firsthand-review and passive-conduit provisions, was disputed as prohibiting Angie’s List from taking provider payments to alter rankings and review visibility.
scopes.why: The firsthand-review and passive-conduit provisions elsewhere in the Membership Agreement are needed to construe the no-endorsement language as prohibiting paid alterations of rankings and review visibility.

scopes.issue: The phrases “other agreements and instruments executed and delivered” and “entire agreement between the parties relating to the subject matter hereof” were lexically ambiguous as to whether related written agreements were incorporated into an expanded agreement and forum-selection scope or the clause merely barred prior parol evidence.
scopes.why: Section 5.9 is needed to see the forum-selection provision whose scope the merger clause allegedly expands; the quoted merger clause alone does not mention forum selection.

scopes.issue: The phrase “transactions contemplated hereby” was lexically disputed as referring only to the auction procedures under the Broker-Dealer Agreement or more broadly to transactions distinct from the Agreement, potentially including the bonds and later swaps.
scopes.why: The Agreement’s recitals and auction provisions are needed to identify the bonds, issuance, and auction procedures that may constitute the “transactions contemplated hereby.”

scopes.issue: The phrase “arising out of” was lexically disputed as requiring claims to originate from and bear a causal connection with the Broker-Dealer Agreement, rather than arise from a separate advisory relationship, including with respect to the 2006 swaps.
scopes.needs: FINRA Statement of Claim,Complaint,and materials concerning the 2006 swaps and alleged advisory relationship
scopes.why: The clause does not reveal what Presbyterian Healthcare’s claims concern or whether the alleged advisory relationship and swaps originate from and bear a causal connection to the Broker-Dealer Agreement.

scopes.issue: The term “all actions and proceedings” was lexically open to whether it encompassed FINRA arbitration or only judicial litigation, while still covering Presbyterian Healthcare’s federal-court action.
scopes.why: The possible limitation of “all actions and proceedings” to judicial matters is visible from its juxtaposition with a United States District Court forum and a jury-trial waiver.

scopes.issue: The wording “all actions and proceedings ... shall be brought” was disputed as mandatory and exclusive venue language rather than a permissive authorization to litigate in New York.
scopes.why: The mandatory-versus-permissive issue appears directly in the command that covered actions and proceedings “shall be brought” in the specified court.

scopes.issue: The promise that the parties “shall submit to the exclusive jurisdiction of the State of New York” was in whole-contract tension with the Endorsement’s submission to “any court of competent jurisdiction,” and the court held that the Endorsement supplanted the New York forum requirement.
scopes.why: The quoted New York-exclusive clause does not reveal the tension without the same Policy’s Service of Suit Endorsement allowing submission to any court of competent jurisdiction.

scopes.issue: The promise to “submit to the jurisdiction of any court of competent jurisdiction” was disputed as either merely conveying personal jurisdiction or, when the Policy was read as a whole, amending the New York-exclusive forum-selection clause to let the insured choose any competent court.
scopes.why: The quoted submission clause requires the same Policy’s New York-exclusive forum clause and the Endorsement’s amendment language to show the disputed effect on forum selection.

scopes.issue: The preservation language “OTHER THAN AS ABOVE STATED” created a whole-contract coherence question over whether the Endorsement could vary the Policy, and the court read it to permit the stated service-of-suit terms to amend the forum-selection clause.
scopes.why: The phrase “OTHER THAN AS ABOVE STATED” requires the preceding Service of Suit terms and the underlying Policy’s forum-selection clause to reveal what the Endorsement may alter.

scopes.issue: The phrase “direct physical loss or damage” was alleged to be lexically ambiguous between any physical alteration, including cosmetic hail dents, and only damage measurably reducing the property’s usefulness or function.
scopes.why: The phrase “direct physical loss or damage” itself carries the alleged choice between any physical alteration and only functionally significant damage.

scopes.issue: The general “physical loss or damage” grant was alleged under ejusdem generis to be narrowed by the supposedly more specific real-property “covered loss” provisions, creating a general-versus-specific scope problem even though no specific enumeration preceded the general grant.
scopes.why: The alleged general-versus-specific conflict and absence of an enumerated-list structure can be seen only by comparing the Insuring Agreement with the policy’s real-property coverage and “covered loss” provisions.

scopes.issue: The phrase “covered loss” in the real-property coverage grant was alleged to be lexically ambiguous between requiring functional or financial loss and encompassing cosmetic dents as an undesirable outcome or financial detriment.
scopes.why: Because “covered loss” is expressly defined elsewhere in the policy, the reader needs that definition—particularly its use of “a loss”—to see the alleged ambiguity.

scopes.issue: The real-property grant’s allegedly more specific “covered loss” wording was asserted to control the general “physical loss or damage” grant under ejusdem generis, although the policy lacked the required specific enumeration followed by general language.
scopes.why: The asserted limitation requires comparing the real-property grant with the Insuring Agreement and examining the policy for the enumeration-and-general-term structure required by ejusdem generis.

scopes.issue: The undefined words “a loss” within the “covered loss” definition were alleged to be lexically ambiguous between an outcome requiring functional damage and an undesirable outcome or financial detriment that could include cosmetic hail dents.
scopes.why: The definition itself leaves “a loss” undefined, exposing the alleged competing meanings of functional damage and an undesirable or financially detrimental outcome.

scopes.issue: The “covered loss” definition was asserted to be the specific provision limiting the broader general grant of “physical loss or damage,” but the court found no enumerated-list and general-term structure supporting ejusdem generis.
scopes.why: The alleged specific-over-general limitation and the absence of an ejusdem-generis list structure require comparison with the policy’s broader “physical loss or damage” grant.

scopes.issue: The rule that a prior sexual relationship “does not constitute consent” was read as making the relationship irrelevant, creating whole-contract tension with the same clause’s rule that consent may be communicated through actions; the court concluded that the relationship was not itself consent but remained central context for evaluating consent.
scopes.why: The clause itself both permits consent to be communicated through actions and says a prior sexual relationship does not itself constitute consent, exposing the stated tension.

scopes.issue: The general prohibition on conduct that “physically harms or is considered unwanted physical contact,” set against examples of “hitting, pushing, or physical altercations/violence,” created a list-scope problem over whether nonviolent unwanted sexual contact constituted “violence.”
scopes.why: The clause itself juxtaposes the broad category of unwanted physical contact with examples involving hitting, pushing, and physical violence.

scopes.issue: Section 17.4’s educational-record access right and incorporation of the University Records Policy had to be read with the Special Examiner records-retention clause to determine whether the Special Examiner’s Report was an educational record accessible within 45 days.
scopes.needs: Brandeis University Records Policy,incorporated by reference but not filed
scopes.why: The filed handbook does not contain the incorporated policy’s 45-day access rule needed to determine the stated deadline.

scopes.issue: Section 19.5’s statement that access to disciplinary records is governed by the University Records Policy had to be read through section 22.6’s incorporation to determine whether John was entitled to timely access to the Special Examiner’s Report.
scopes.needs: Brandeis University Records Policy,incorporated by reference but not filed
scopes.why: The incorporated policy is needed to supply the timely-access requirement, including the 45-day period, that section 19.5 does not state.

scopes.issue: Section 19.6.j applies by its terms to a “Written Hearing Report,” creating a whole-contract coherence problem because section 22.6 expressly incorporates it even though the Special Examiner Process has no hearing and produces no Hearing Report.
scopes.why: The coherence problem appears only by comparing this Hearing Report provision with section 22.6’s incorporation of it into the hearingless Special Examiner Process.

scopes.issue: The general term “the case,” following the enumerated trigger of one or more possible Section 3 or Section 7 violations, created a list-scope dispute over whether mixed sexual and nonsexual charges required separate proceedings or all belonged in the Special Examiner Process.
scopes.why: The clause itself follows the enumerated Section 3 or 7 trigger with the broader phrase “the case,” exposing the scope question for mixed charges.

scopes.issue: The Special Examiner’s authority to “make[] a finding” of responsibility had to be harmonized with the panel’s later authority over “outcomes” and the appeal provision’s reference to a panel “final decision” to determine whether the examiner’s responsibility finding was final.
scopes.why: The finality of the examiner’s responsibility finding cannot be assessed without the same handbook’s provisions governing panel outcomes and appeals.

scopes.issue: The direction that a responsible finding moves the process to deliberations had to be read with the provisions assigning the panel only outcome recommendations and the Special Examiner the responsibility finding, resolving whether deliberations could revisit responsibility.
scopes.why: The clause only directs a responsible finding into deliberations, so the panel’s limited outcome authority and the examiner’s responsibility authority must be read elsewhere in the handbook.

scopes.issue: The clause saying the panel makes “recommendations” and the SSAO renders the “final decision” was in tension with the appeal clause’s statement that the panel makes a “final decision.”
scopes.why: The conflict requires comparison with the appeal provision, which attributes a “final decision” to the panel despite this clause assigning it only recommendations.

scopes.issue: The panel’s authority to recommend “outcome(s)” created a whole-contract coherence dispute over whether “outcomes” meant a responsibility finding plus sanctions, as John argued, or sanctions alone, as Brandeis argued.
scopes.why: Determining whether “outcome(s)” includes responsibility requires the handbook’s separate allocations of responsibility findings and sanctions.

scopes.issue: The Outcome Notification provision’s use of both “final outcome(s) decision” and “sanctions” created whole-contract uncertainty whether “outcome” and “sanction” were synonymous or sanction was only a subset of outcome.
scopes.why: The clause itself uses “final outcome(s) decision” and “sanctions” separately without explaining whether the latter exhaust or merely form part of the former.

scopes.issue: The appeal provision’s reference to an “imposed sanction,” rather than an “outcome,” contributed to whole-contract uncertainty whether sanctions and outcomes were the same or whether sanctions were a subset of outcomes.
scopes.why: The significance of using “sanction” rather than “outcome” appears only when this appeal language is compared with the handbook’s outcome provisions.

scopes.issue: The statement that the parties could appeal the panel’s “final decision” conflicted with the Deliberations Phase provision under which the panel merely recommended outcomes and the SSAO rendered the final decision.
scopes.why: The stated conflict requires the Deliberations Phase provision assigning the panel recommendations and the SSAO/D the final decision.

scopes.issue: The provision retaining Special Examiner documents “pursuant to” sections 17.4, 19.5, and 19.6.j required those cross-referenced provisions to be read together to decide whether John could access the Special Examiner’s Report within 45 days.
scopes.needs: Brandeis University Records Policy,incorporated by reference but not filed
scopes.why: Although the cross-referenced handbook sections identify access rights, the unfiled incorporated policy supplies the 45-day access period.

scopes.issue: The express incorporation of section 19.6.j created a whole-contract coherence defect because that section governs a Written Hearing Report, while the Special Examiner Process has no hearing and generates no such report.
scopes.why: The defect appears by reading this incorporation together with section 19.6.j and the Special Examiner provisions showing that no hearing or Written Hearing Report exists.

scopes.issue: Although “Policy Value” was not expressly listed in Paragraph A, “Net Amount at Risk” incorporated Policy Value through the policy’s separate NAR definition, so Paragraph A could be understood only by reading those provisions together.
scopes.why: The separate Net Amount at Risk definition is needed to see that the listed NAR factor incorporates Policy Value.

scopes.issue: The scope of “as of the Policy Date” was unclear until Paragraph A was construed together with Paragraph B, which made Paragraph A govern only the initial COI rate and Paragraph B govern subsequent Policy-Month adjustments.
scopes.why: Paragraph B’s separate treatment of rates for a Policy Month is needed to limit Paragraph A to the initial rate on the Policy Date.

scopes.issue: The phrase “based on” was lexically ambiguous between Fleisher’s exhaustive reading, limiting adjustments to the six enumerated factors, and Phoenix’s illustrative reading, allowing additional relevant factors.
scopes.why: The words “based on” followed by a specific list themselves permit the competing exhaustive and illustrative readings.

scopes.issue: The undefined term “mortality” was disputed as potentially incorporating Policy Values, but the court gave it the settled insurance-industry meaning of actuarially predicted frequency of death, which has nothing to do with Policy Values.
scopes.why: The clause uses “mortality” without elaboration, and its settled insurance-industry meaning is available as general knowledge.

scopes.issue: The undefined term “persistency” was disputed as potentially meaning either “policy persistency” or “premium persistency” and thereby incorporating Policy Values, rather than its ordinary insurance meaning of the percentage of policies that have not lapsed.
scopes.why: The clause’s unqualified use of “persistency” carries the asserted uncertainty between policy and premium persistency, while its ordinary insurance meaning is general knowledge.

scopes.issue: The phrase “expectations of ... investment earnings” was disputed between Fleisher’s proposed meaning of the investment “spread” or net rate of return and Phoenix’s meaning of predicted investment income, under which Policy Values logically affect the amount available to invest.
scopes.why: The phrase “expectations of ... investment earnings” itself presents the disputed contrast between investment income and investment spread or rate of return.

scopes.issue: The reference to a “specific Policy Month” was construed together with Paragraph A’s separate reference to the “Policy Date,” resulting in Paragraph B governing COI-rate adjustments after the initial rate was set.
scopes.why: Paragraph A’s separate reference to rates “as of the Policy Date” is needed to construe Paragraph B’s reference to a “specific Policy Month” as governing later adjustments.

scopes.issue: The undefined phrase “discriminate unfairly” was vague as to which differential treatment was prohibited, and the court construed it to mean discrimination lacking a proper underwriting basis under generally accepted actuarial standards.
scopes.why: The clause does not specify what makes discrimination “unfair,” and the governing statutory and actuarial meaning is legal and industry background rather than case-specific material.

scopes.issue: The phrase “class of insureds” was vague about whether classes had to be fixed at policy issuance or Phoenix could later subdivide the issued PAUL series by age and face amount.
scopes.why: The phrase “any class of insureds” contains no rule stating when a class must be fixed or whether it may later be subdivided.

scopes.issue: The requirement to keep an “all risk policy of insurance” was disputed as to whether policies covering the Premises merely as an empty building could satisfy it, a lexical scope question the court resolved by holding that the wording unambiguously required all-risk coverage.
scopes.why: The clause itself requires an “all risk” policy covering both Tenant’s personal property and all buildings and improvements, exposing whether empty-building coverage falls short.

scopes.issue: The indemnity for claims arising from an “accident, injury or damage” to property was disputed as to whether its broad wording covered Islip’s attorney’s fees in this interparty litigation or only third-party claims, and the court held it clearly addressed third-party claims.
scopes.why: The clause’s accident, injury, property-damage, and claim-or-proceeding language itself exposes the question whether the attorney-fee indemnity is limited to third-party claims rather than interparty litigation.

scopes.issue: The indemnity for “[a]ny breach of Tenant’s representations or warranties” was disputed as to whether it covered Islip’s attorney’s fees from Gander Mountain’s earlier challenge to the Lease’s validity or instead contemplated third-party warranty claims, and the court found no wording unequivocally referring to claims between the contracting parties.
scopes.why: The reader must examine the Tenant’s representations and warranties elsewhere in the Lease, particularly the warranty that the Lease is valid and binding, to connect the indemnity trigger to the earlier validity challenge and assess its interparty reach.

scopes.issue: The provision that Landlord “shall not have any right to accelerate” rent was disputed as to whether Islip could nevertheless recover future rents or their present value by labeling them damages for Gander Mountain’s anticipatory total breach, and the court held that the wording barred recovery of future rent before it accrued.
scopes.why: The clause expressly preserves liability for future rent as it accrues while categorically denying Landlord any right to accelerate rent, directly exposing the attempted recovery of unaccrued rent under another label.

scopes.issue: The scope of “governed by the substantive laws ... of the State of Wyoming” was disputed as to whether it also made Wyoming law govern the threshold choice-of-law inquiry, which the court held it did not expressly do.
scopes.why: The wording selects Wyoming’s substantive law but does not expressly state that Wyoming law governs the threshold choice-of-law inquiry.

scopes.issue: Brenner challenged “any dispute” as lexically ambiguous, but offered no competing reading and the court rejected the asserted ambiguity.
scopes.why: The asserted lexical ambiguity is carried by the clause’s own phrase “any dispute,” without requiring another provision or document.

scopes.issue: The breadth of “any mediation or suit” was disputed as to whether it included wrongful-death and negligence claims based on duties allegedly arising outside the Agreement, and the court construed it to include those tort claims.
scopes.why: The breadth of “any mediation or suit” itself raises whether the forum requirement encompasses tort claims arising outside the Agreement.

scopes.issue: The phrase requiring suit “only in the State of Wyoming” did not specify federal or state court, and the court construed it to permit suit in either court located there.
scopes.why: The clause specifies only a geographic location—“in the State of Wyoming”—without choosing between federal and state court.

scopes.issue: The relationship between the first two sentences and the minimum-proceeds sentence was unclear because Dorchester read the latter as modifying the actual-proceeds formula to require the highest obtainable price, while Chesapeake read it as modifying the transportation-expense provision immediately preceding it.
scopes.why: The quoted clause omits the minimum-proceeds sentence whose relationship to the first two sentences creates the stated ambiguity, so the rest of paragraph 3(b) in the same lease is required.

scopes.issue: The undefined phrase “field or prevailing area” was lexically ambiguous because Dorchester treated “field” and “prevailing area” as two different localities, whereas Chesapeake treated them as a single, roughly synonymous geographic term.
scopes.why: The clause itself uses the undefined phrase “field or prevailing area,” whose wording permits either two distinct localities or one synonymous geographic term.

scopes.issue: The minimum-proceeds sentence lacked whole-contract coherence because its highest-price and transportation-protection readings remained in tension when compared with the preceding gas-royalty sentences, the oil-royalty formula, the payment deadline, and the plant-processed-gas provision’s cross-reference to it.
scopes.why: The stated defect depends on comparing the minimum-proceeds sentence with paragraphs 3(a), 3(b), 3(d), and 3(h) of the same lease.

scopes.issue: The whole-contract scope question was whether “dispute,” covering “all federal or state law claims” arising “directly or indirectly” from the Agreement and claims asserted as a class representative or member, encompassed Pond’s class claims stemming from the loan and the ensuing bounced-check prosecution.
scopes.needs: Pond’s complaint allegations and criminal-check proceeding facts
scopes.why: The clause supplies the definition of “dispute,” but the reader needs case-specific allegations to know that Pond’s class claims stemmed from the loan and ensuing bounced-check prosecution.

scopes.issue: The whole-contract scope question was whether “Claim,” broadly defined to cover disputes arising from the Agreement and the parties’ or third parties’ actions, including claims for money damages, penalties, or equitable relief, encompassed Vine’s claims arising indirectly from the loan and related criminal-check proceedings.
scopes.needs: Vine’s complaint allegations and criminal-check proceeding facts
scopes.why: The clause defines “Claim” broadly, but the reader needs case-specific allegations to determine whether Vine’s claims arose from the loan and related criminal-check proceedings.

scopes.issue: The “Continued Performance” provision was disputed as to whether it qualified as an “other provision relating to dispute resolution” incorporated into the Guaranty, and the court held that it did because the Guaranty contained no separate continued-performance provision.
scopes.needs: 252FSupp3d52_guaranty_agreement
scopes.why: Without the Guaranty, the reader cannot see the residual incorporation language or that the Guaranty contains no separate continued-performance provision.

scopes.issue: The heading “Governing Law, Jurisdiction, Venue and Forum” was argued to make §4.6’s placement incompatible with creating a dispute-related performance covenant, but the court read the section’s substance and the entire Guaranty as controlling over that organizational label.
scopes.why: The argument turns on comparing §4.6’s organizational heading with the dispute-resolution substance elsewhere in that section and the Guaranty’s separate Covenants and Agreements article.

scopes.issue: The phrase “All other provisions relating to dispute resolution or arbitration” was disputed as to whether it incorporated Network Operator Agreement §11.2 despite §4.6’s differing dispute procedures, and the court construed the specific variations as carve-outs while giving the residual incorporation language effect.
scopes.needs: 252FSupp3d52_agreement_for_network_operator
scopes.why: The referenced Network Operator Agreement is needed to identify §11.2 as a continued-performance provision and compare its dispute-resolution scheme with the Guaranty’s specific procedures.

scopes.issue: The phrase “subject to annual review for adjustment at the discretion of the Board,” together with the scheduled next adjustment, was alleged to require a salary review or adjustment but was construed as unambiguously giving the Board discretion not to consider or modify Lankau’s compensation.
scopes.why: The clause itself juxtaposes mandatory-sounding annual review and a scheduled adjustment date with the qualification “at the discretion of the Board,” creating the stated dispute over whether review or adjustment is required.

scopes.issue: The parenthetical “subject to approval by the Board and the Corporation’s policies” was facially ambiguous because it could modify Lankau’s eligibility for an individual equity grant, as Luxoft argued, or refer only to Board approval of SOP III, as Lankau argued.
scopes.why: The parenthetical’s placement after “eligible to participate in the Stock Option Plan” facially permits competing readings as to whether Board approval governs individual participation or the plan itself.

scopes.issue: The phrase “oil and/or gas” presented a lexical scope dispute over whether “gas” included liquid NGLs, which the court held it did not under the term’s ordinary meaning.
scopes.why: The clause itself limits royalties to proceeds from “oil and/or gas,” and the ordinary meaning of “gas” supplies the stated lexical dispute over whether that term includes liquid NGLs.

scopes.issue: The modifier “of a Financial Instrument” in “Forgery or alteration of a Financial Instrument” was lexically disputed over whether it applied only to “alteration,” permitting standalone forgery coverage, or to both “Forgery” and “alteration,” requiring corruption of a Financial Instrument.
scopes.why: The coordination in “Forgery or alteration of a Financial Instrument” itself permits a dispute over whether the trailing modifier applies to both nouns or only to “alteration.”

scopes.issue: The words “direct loss ... resulting from Computer Fraud” were lexically disputed over whether the spoofed emails directly caused Medidata’s loss despite the intervening telephone calls and employees’ approval of the wire transfer.
scopes.needs: Evidence of the spoofed emails,telephone calls,and employee wire approvals
scopes.why: Without the transaction’s sequence of communications and approvals, a reader cannot assess whether intervening acts broke the direct causal connection required by the clause.

scopes.issue: The phrase “change to Data elements or program logic” was lexically disputed over whether the thief’s code changed data from the true email address to Medidata’s president’s address or Gmail merely populated the email normally.
scopes.needs: Joint Factual Stipulation Following Discovery (ECF 72) and email-system evidence
scopes.why: A reader needs the case-specific operation of the thief’s code, SMTP and IMF fields, and Gmail processing to determine whether data was changed or merely populated normally.

scopes.issue: The phrase “fraudulent ... entry of Data into ... a Computer System” was lexically disputed over whether spoofed emails sent to an inbox open to the public constituted covered deceitful and dishonest access or merely authorized submission of fraudulent content.
scopes.needs: Joint Factual Stipulation Following Discovery (ECF 72) and email-system access evidence
scopes.why: Whether the spoofed messages amounted to deceitful access rather than authorized submission of false content depends on how Medidata’s inbox and Gmail system accepted and processed them.

scopes.issue: The definition of “Forgery” as “the signing of the name of another” was lexically disputed over whether spoofed emails containing Medidata’s president’s name constituted a forgery, although the court did not resolve that reading.
scopes.needs: The spoofed emails and evidence of how the president’s name appeared
scopes.why: The clause alone does not show whether the case-specific emails displayed the president’s name in a manner that could constitute his electronic signing.

scopes.issue: The phrase “purportedly issued by an Organization” was lexically disputed over whether wire instructions entered and sent by Medidata employees were actually issued by Medidata or remained purported instructions because the employees acted through the impostor’s trick.
scopes.needs: Evidence of the impostor’s communications and employees’ wire instructions
scopes.why: Whether the instructions were actually or only purportedly issued by Medidata depends on who created and transmitted the operative instructions and how the impostor induced them.

scopes.issue: The phrase “without such Organization’s knowledge or consent” was lexically disputed over whether the employees’ willing approval supplied Medidata’s knowledge and consent or whether knowledge and consent obtained only by trick were ineffective.
scopes.needs: Evidence of the deception and employees’ approval of the wire transfer
scopes.why: A reader needs the circumstances of the employees’ knowledge, approval, and reliance on the impostor to decide whether Medidata’s knowledge or consent was supplied or defeated by trick.

scopes.issue: The limitation of “then-current hourly rates” to approved additional services outside the Scope of Services was in whole-contract tension with Jernigan Copeland’s reading that the regular monthly retainer was also billed against hours, and instead supported the flat-fee reading.
scopes.why: The tension arises only by comparing the additional-services hourly-rate limitation with the regular Scope of Services and section 4.1’s monthly-retainer provision.

scopes.issue: The sixty-day written-termination provision would be meaningless under the advance-hourly reading of the monthly retainer because the Client could stop work, and therefore compensation, at any time under the separate stop-work provision.
scopes.why: The termination clause becomes allegedly meaningless only when compared with the separate stop-work right and the disputed compensation provisions.

scopes.issue: The phrase “monthly retainer of $30,000” presented alleged lexical ambiguity between a flat fee payable each month regardless of the amount of work and an advance-fee security retainer drawn down only for recorded billable time.
scopes.why: The clause itself juxtaposes a “monthly retainer of $30,000” with tracking all hours and supplying details with invoices, carrying the competing flat-fee and advance-retainer readings.

scopes.issue: When read as a whole with the hours-tracking, invoicing, additional-services, termination, and stop-work provisions, the “monthly retainer” language was disputed as an advance deposit but construed as a flat monthly fee that gave effect to the Contract’s other terms.
scopes.why: The whole-contract dispute requires comparison with the invoicing, additional-services, termination, and stop-work provisions.

scopes.issue: The requirement for monthly invoices “detailing its fees and expenses” was disputed as evidence of an hourly advance retainer, but in whole-contract context the Court construed the invoices as an accounting and payment mechanism consistent with a flat monthly fee.
scopes.why: Whether invoices are hourly drawdowns or merely accounting and payment mechanisms depends on section 4.1’s retainer language and the more detailed invoicing terms elsewhere in the Agreement.

scopes.issue: The word “Services” was disputed as requiring actual logged work after May 1 rather than also encompassing Xenophon’s contractual availability of staff through the Contract’s expiration.
scopes.why: The contrast between actual logged work and compensable staff availability through expiration requires the Agreement’s flat-fee, staffing, scope-of-services, and termination provisions.

scopes.issue: The promise that Starr, “at your request, will submit to the jurisdiction of a court of competent jurisdiction within the United States” was tested for facial lexical ambiguity over whether it let TriUnion choose the forum, and the court held that it unambiguously did so.

scopes.issue: The Service of Suit promise was in whole-contract tension with the original New York forum-selection clause, requiring the court to decide whether the endorsement modified that clause to permit suit in TriUnion’s chosen forum.
scopes.why: The conflict and modification issue requires comparison of the Service of Suit promise with the original New York forum-selection provision elsewhere in the same policy.

scopes.issue: The statement that “[a]ll other terms and conditions” remained unchanged posed a whole-contract coherence question over whether the preceding Service of Suit terms changed the original forum-selection clause or left it intact.

scopes.why: The reader must inspect the rest of Section 10 to see that it contains no express warranties made by Accredited and that MSMC’s reading would therefore leave the quoted backstop procedure without operation.

scopes.issue: The disputed lexical scope of “all further obligations” was whether it meant only obligations under the employment contract or every obligation between the parties, including the separate Miami University buyout agreement.
scopes.why: The unqualified phrase “all further obligations” itself raises whether its reach is confined to this Contract or extends to every obligation owed to the Employee.

scopes.issue: The meaning of “all further obligations” presented a whole-contract coherence issue because provisions 14.4 and 14.10 use “hereunder” to limit obligations to the employment contract, while provision 14.1 contains no comparable limiting language.
scopes.why: The coherence issue cannot be seen without comparing provision 14.1’s unqualified wording with the limiting word “hereunder” used in provisions 14.4 and 14.10 of the same contract.

scopes.issue: The definition’s phrase “progeny, portions, unmodified derivatives and any accompanying know-how or data” was facially ambiguous as to whether a near-exact copy modified for a lentiviral vector was a “portion” of the Campana Construct or an excluded modified derivative requiring no physical part of the transferred construct.
scopes.why: The juxtaposition of broad “portions” with specifically limited “unmodified derivatives” makes the treatment of a modified near-copy uncertain from the definition itself.

scopes.issue: The phrase “product that contains Material” was facially ambiguous as to whether a product containing a copied and modified sequence counted as containing Material or had to contain a physical part of the construct St. Jude transferred.
scopes.why: The phrase “contains Material” cannot reveal the stated ambiguity without the same agreement’s definition of “Material,” including “portions” and “unmodified derivatives.”},{

scopes.why: The juxtaposition of broad “portions” with specifically limited “unmodified derivatives” makes the treatment of a modified near-copy uncertain from the definition itself.

scopes.issue: The description of Penn producing “a molecular lentiviral vector clone incorporating Materials” left unclear whether the resulting clone was itself within “Materials,” as St. Jude’s theory implied, or was a distinct modified product merely incorporating Materials, as Penn argued.
scopes.why: Determining whether the clone produced by incorporating “Materials” is itself within that term requires the same agreement’s definition of “Materials.”

scopes.issue: The alternatives “contains a portion of the Materials,” “is derived from the Materials,” and “could not have been produced but for” them were facially ambiguous in application to the June Construct, which copied and modified the sequence but contained no physical part of the construct St. Jude supplied.
scopes.why: Applying the three alternatives to a copied and modified sequence requires the same agreement’s definition of “Materials,” particularly its treatment of portions and derivatives.

scopes.issue: The transfer command that CollaGenex “shall transfer to Skold the Purchased Assets” was vague because it specified no date, leaving unclear whether transfer was required immediately upon termination or at some later time.
scopes.why: The transfer command itself contains no deadline or timing standard for when CollaGenex must complete the transfer.

scopes.issue: The phrase “either Party may, by written notice to the other, require” mediation was disputed as either imposing mandatory mediation before suit or merely permitting a party to request nonbinding mediation, with the court adopting the permissive reading.
scopes.why: The clause itself uses the permissive “may” while describing a party’s ability to “require” mediation, making the disputed mandatory-versus-permissive effect visible from its wording.

scopes.issue: The scope of “any controversy arising hereunder” was disputed as potentially limited to contractual claims, but the court construed it to cover noncontractual claims that arise from the contractual relationship and implicate the Agreement’s terms.
scopes.why: The phrase “any controversy arising hereunder” itself presents the disputed question whether the forum provision reaches only contractual claims or also related noncontractual claims.
